clinicalPearls: Ureaplasma urealyticum is a cell-wall-deficient mollicute that colonises the lower genital tract of many sexually active adults, so its detection often reflects commensal carriage rather than disease
Its pathogenic role is debated; unlike Mycoplasma genitalium it is not consistently proven to cause urethritis, and routine testing or treatment of asymptomatic carriers is generally not advised
Ureaplasma urealyticum (as distinct from the usually commensal Ureaplasma parvum) has been implicated in some cases of non-chlamydial non-gonococcal urethritis
In pregnancy, ureaplasmas are associated with chorioamnionitis, preterm birth, and low birth weight, and they can be transmitted vertically to the neonate
In preterm and very-low-birth-weight infants, respiratory tract colonisation has been linked to neonatal pneumonia and to the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Because it lacks a cell wall, it is invisible on Gram stain and inherently resistant to beta-lactams; diagnosis uses culture on specialised media or nucleic acid amplification testing
When treatment is genuinely indicated, macrolides such as azithromycin or a tetracycline such as doxycycline are typically used, though tetracycline resistance occurs
Interpreting a positive result requires clinical correlation, since a detection alone does not establish causation
reference.pathophysiology: Ureaplasma species are among the smallest free-living bacteria and, like other mollicutes, lack a cell wall; they are named for their capacity to hydrolyse urea as an energy source. They frequently colonise the urogenital mucosa as commensals, and the balance between harmless carriage and disease appears to depend on host factors, bacterial load, species and serovar, and the presence of co-pathogens. When pathogenic, urease-driven ammonia production and a local inflammatory response are thought to contribute to mucosal injury, and the same mechanisms are implicated in intra-amniotic infection when the organism ascends in pregnancy, provoking chorioamnionitis and inflammation that may precipitate preterm labour and injure the developing fetal lung. Neonatal colonisation, particularly in preterm infants, can be followed by respiratory disease and chronic lung injury.
additionalInvestigations: Nucleic acid amplification testing or specialised culture of genital or urine specimens, with species differentiation where available
Concurrent nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea to exclude established pathogens
Microscopy of genital smears to document urethritis or cervicitis
Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis in persistent urethritis
In relevant pregnancy or neonatal settings, placental histology or neonatal respiratory sampling as clinically indicated
Screening for other sexually transmitted infections when a sexually acquired cause is suspected
redFlags: Preterm labour, prelabour rupture of membranes, or clinical chorioamnionitis in pregnancy
Respiratory deterioration in a colonised preterm neonate suggesting pneumonia or evolving chronic lung disease
Persistent symptomatic urethritis despite treatment for established pathogens
Systemic or invasive infection in an immunocompromised host
reference.prognosis: In most immunocompetent adults ureaplasma carriage is benign and needs no treatment; when genuine infection is treated the outlook is generally good, whereas perinatal infection carries a less favourable outlook because of its associations with preterm birth and neonatal respiratory morbidity.
pitfalls: Treating an asymptomatic positive result and mistaking commensal colonisation for disease
Failing to exclude established pathogens such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and Mycoplasma genitalium before attributing symptoms to ureaplasma
Prescribing a beta-lactam, which is ineffective against a cell-wall-deficient organism
Overlooking the perinatal implications of ureaplasma in pregnant and preterm-neonatal populations
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
BASHH UK guidance on non-gonococcal urethritis and genital mollicutes
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
management: Do not test or treat asymptomatic urogenital carriage, which usually represents commensal colonisation rather than disease
Treat genuine symptomatic infection with a macrolide (azithromycin) or a tetracycline (doxycycline), reserving fluoroquinolones for treatment failure
Avoid beta-lactams, which are inherently ineffective because the organism lacks a cell wall
Test for and treat co-existing established pathogens (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Mycoplasma genitalium) in non-gonococcal urethritis
Arrange partner notification, contact treatment and a full sexually transmitted infection screen when infection is sexually acquired

In pregnancy manage chorioamnionitis and preterm-labour risk, and treat colonised preterm or very-low-birth-weight neonates with pneumonia or evolving bronchopulmonary dysplasia using a macrolide, with obstetric and neonatal specialist input
